segments.line: Here's what happened.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach us. That's real.
But today, light was halving faster than it could make the trip.
Any sunlight that left the Sun after about ten twenty this morning will never arrive. The Sun
didn't go out. Earth just got cut off from it.
And sunlight isn't only light. It's heat. Almost all the warmth on Earth's surface comes from it. Scientists at Caltech worked out what happens without it.
Within about a week, the surface drops below freezing.
Within a year, to about minus seventy degrees. That's real.
No sunlight also means no plants growing. No crops. No food. Not this year, not ever.
Then the signals go.
GPS satellites fly about twenty thousand kilometers up. That's real.
Your phone finds you by timing their signals to a billionth of a second, at the speed of light. Today, that speed changes
every hour. Every map on Earth points to the wrong place.
Ships, planes and delivery trucks stop where they are.
A taxi driver follows his map straight into a lake. He's fine. His taxi isn't. At
home, your mom tapes blankets over the windows to keep the heat in. The
whole family drags their mattresses into the living room, around the one electric heater.
Ellie asks when the Sun is coming back.
Nobody answers her. At
midnight, a phone call to the other side of the world takes almost two hours to arrive. The
internet is still there. It just takes all night to load a page. And
at three in the morning, light becomes slower than sound.
That's three hundred and forty meters a second. That's real.
If you clapped your hands in the dark, you would hear the clap before you saw it.
Outside, it's already colder than any morning this time of year. And
every hour, it gets worse.
